source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Preeclampsia with severe features because persistent severe headache and visual symptoms qualify as severe features.","B":"Preeclampsia without severe features because the blood pressure has not reached the severe range of 160/110 mm Hg.","C":"Gestational hypertension with severe features because proteinuria does not change the hypertensive diagnosis.","D":"Chronic hypertension with superimposed preeclampsia because hypertension first appeared during this pregnancy."}}
source_row.rationale: ACOG describes preeclampsia as hypertension arising after 20 weeks with findings such as proteinuria and identifies severe headache and visual changes as severe features. Option A is therefore the best classification even though the blood pressure itself is below the severe-range threshold. Option B incorrectly ignores severe neurologic features. Option C is inferior because proteinuria supports preeclampsia rather than isolated gestational hypertension. Option D is incorrect because chronic hypertension is present before pregnancy or develops before 20 weeks, not first recognized at 32 weeks in a previously normotensive client.

source_row.stem: A previously normotensive pregnant client at 32 weeks has repeated blood pressures of 148/94 mm Hg, new proteinuria, a severe headache that persists despite medication, and visual spots. Which classification is most accurate?
